title: The sisters' songs
hookLine: the poems of the first nuns, kept in the Pali canon in their own voices

lines: A KITCHEN, A LAMP, A ROBE.
cards: A woman remembers her kitchen and says she's free of it. Another watches a lamp go out. Another is told she can finally sleep.
Another left her room again and again before she could sit still. Until now the path has told stories about the women of the early sangha. Now they speak.
In a small book of the Pali canon, the nuns of the Buddha's time talk about their own lives, their losses and their freedom, in verse.

teach.b: First, the name. Therigatha. A theri is an elder nun, a senior woman of the order.
A gatha is a verse. So the title is simply the verses of the elder nuns. Second, the verse.
They're short poems, some only a few lines, some much longer, each put in the mouth of a nun, usually named. Some are her own words about her life and how she came free.

Some are words spoken to her, by the Buddha or a teacher, that the collection keeps as hers. Third, her own voice. The poems talk about kitchen tools, husbands, children lost, a body growing old, a restless night, a lamp.
Awakening here doesn't happen far away from ordinary life. It happens in the middle of it, and the women say so plainly, sometimes with grief, sometimes with a sharp joke.
Fourth, where they were kept. The Therigatha sits in the Pali canon's collection of shorter books, beside a companion book of verses by elder monks, where the path already met Sunita and Sopaka.

A later commentary adds a life story for each nun, and scholars debate how old each poem is and how the collection came together. Some readers count it among the earliest collections of women's poetry anywhere.
Whatever the dating, the canon kept women of the early sangha speaking about their own awakening, in the first person, and handed their words down.

how: The Therigatha is read and studied by Buddhists and scholars as the voices of the early nuns, and its verses are recited in Pali in some Theravada communities and quoted in talks about women's place in the sangha.

games.q: you're a nun of the early sangha, and you've come free. the community wants to remember it. what is kept?
o: a new rule for the order.
a few lines of verse, in your own voice.
games.why: the Therigatha keeps short poems in the nuns' own voices, and the canon handed them down.

practice: Read one short poem slowly, once, aloud and quietly if you can: one from a book on your shelf, one a friend sent, one you remember from school. Choose the line that stays, and sit with it without explaining it to yourself.
Let it repeat, the way, tradition says, the nuns' verses were recited and remembered before anyone wrote them down.
